Two Artifacts, One Line of Growth | Analysis, synthesis, evaluation, and reflection across a creative project and a research report | 2 | ARTIFACT ONE  |  CREATIVE WRITING | Lenora, oh, Lenora | Creative project: fiction following Lenora, a dancer, through mental health, friendship, and belongingLiterary analysis of my own experience became deliberate craft choicesPOV, voice, and imagery solve communication problems | ARTIFACT TWO  |  ACADEMIC RESEARCH | Animal-Assisted Interventions Proposal | Research report: a semester-long campus study of Animal-Assisted Activities and student well-beingClosely examining gaps in the literature turned questions into structured inquiryEvidence, design, and ethics decide what a study can responsibly claim | Interdisciplinary by designI combine multiple sources, analyze, synthesize, evaluate, and reflect. I stopped asking “What does my professor want me to write?” and now ask “What am I trying to understand?” | SLO 2: Communication, Craft, and Creative Problem-Solving | SLO 1: Critical Thinking, Analysis, and Problem-Solving | Writing | Health | Sustainability | Social issues

Lenora’s Struggle to Belong | Center Stage Anxiety | The dance team is not just a setting. It is a community Lenora has invested in. | When tension with teammates makes her place uncertain, close reading shows the scene narrowing around what she notices and what her body is doing. | 3 | THE CRAFT QUESTION | How could I use dialogue and imagery to reveal emotional complexity without explaining every emotion for the reader? | Images on this slide were generated with AI. | A place to contribute | A place to be seen | A place she fears losing

Craft Choices That Carry the Feeling | Structure, POV, voice, and the body do the explaining | 4 | “BPD” | CONTRADICTION AND REPETITION | “Runs away from problems” / “Runs towards problems” / “laughs and cries.” | Episodic, repetitive structure communicates a mental state before anyone explains it. | “Across the Floor” | SECOND-PERSON NARRATION | “You learn early to bring your knee pads.” | Second-person POV puts the reader inside the pressure of dance instead of a safe distance. | “Center Stage Anxiety” | REVISED TOWARD THE BODY | Lenora presses her nails into her palm before she can name what she feels. | Imagery delivers anxiety as physical evidence, not a label. | Techniques are not decoration. Each one solves a communication problem.

How I Wrote That Experience | Dialogue, gesture, and imagery slow the hallway moment down | 1  BREATH: SLOW THE MOMENT | I slow the scene down. Close reading shows it: imagery of uneven breathing keeps readers from rushing past. | 2  GESTURE: SHOW THE SUPPORT | Lain puts his jacket over her shoulders. Dialogue and gesture reveal support before anyone names the emotion. | 3  CHOICE: REVISE THE ENDING | Lenora chooses to walk away from the conflict. Evaluation and revision: belonging does not have to mean staying at any cost. | 5 | HOW THE SCENE BUILDS TOWARD AGENCY | 1  BREATHPacing slows; the reader notices the body | 2  GESTUREAction replaces speech; support is visible | 3  CHOICERevised ending; Lenora walks away for herself | Each step moves the reader from noticing to understanding.

How I Turned a Related Question into Research | Closely examining gaps in AAI research led to the proposed AAA campus program | 6 | Images on this slide were generated with AI. | AAI  |  Animal-Assisted InterventionsThe broader field and umbrella term | AAA  |  Animal-Assisted Activities sessionsThe proposed campus wellness program | PROPOSED DESIGN | WHENSemester-long follow-up | WHOAAA participants + comparison group | HOWRepeated surveys, interviews, and observations | WHAT THE STUDY MEASURES | State anxiety | Trait anxiety | Perceived stress | Emotional well-being | Perceptions of campus support

The Proposed Study at a Glance | Combining multiple sources to build a semester-long, combined-methods campus study | 7 | 100 | undergraduates across four academic classifications | 12–14 | weeks of recurring, bi-weekly sessions | 5 | students at most per session with a therapy dog and handler | 20 | students interviewed, five from each classification | AAI GROUP | Attends bi-weekly small-group sessions with a certified therapy dog and trained handlers in consistent campus locations. | COMPARISON GROUP | Completes the same measurements on the same schedule without attending sessions, so changes can be compared.

Protecting the People in the Study | Ethics is built into the design, and it builds the study’s ethos | 8 | IRB and Belmont principles | IRB approval comes before any recruitment. The study follows respect for persons, beneficence, and justice. | Informed consent | Participants learn the purpose, risks, and time commitment. They can skip questions or withdraw without penalty, and grades and services are never affected. | A distress protocol | Researchers are not crisis counselors. The protocol says when to pause, offers campus and emergency resources, and responds to safety concerns. | Inclusive access | Recruitment states that a dog will be present. Students can decline touching or request distance, and an animal-free wellness option is available.

Three Decisions That Changed My Thinking | Evaluation and reflection: each came from spotting a weakness in my own design | 9 | Add a comparison group | “Because student stress changes naturally during the semester, the design includes a nonparticipating comparison group.” | I could ask whether similar changes happened without the intervention. | Count animal welfare as success | “A program cannot be called successful because students benefit if dogs or handlers are overstressed.” | The program became a system of students, handlers, animals, staff, and resources. | Mix methods for a reason | Numbers show whether scores changed. Interviews and open-ended responses explain why. | Each form of evidence answers a different part of the problem.

My Growth, My Skills, My Goals | From explaining everything to analysis, synthesis, evaluation, and reflection | GROWTH | From explaining to structuring | In fiction, I used to explain every emotion. Now I use dialogue and imagery so readers notice it themselves.In research, I moved from gathering evidence to closely examining gaps in what it does not explain. | SKILLS | What I can now do | Creative problem-solving: choosing genre, POV, and voice on purpose.Analysis and synthesis: close reading and thematic analysis, then combining sources.Evaluation and reflection: re-seeing a whole project, not just editing. | GOALS | Where I am headed | Design a strategy for a specific audience: know what they should notice.Design work that tests whether something helps, instead of forcing a positive conclusion.Keep access, ethics, and community needs in every project. | 10 | Lenora taught me how to give experience structure. The proposal taught me how to give questions structure.

Why It Matters | Both projects taught me to listen closely and take people’s experiences seriously. | Writers shape which experiences become visible through voice and POV.Campuses decide what counts as evidence that support is working. | What does it take to feel supported in a community you’re trying to belong to? | 11 | Images on this slide were generated with AI.
